passage:
I’m Deepika, and I sit behind Tushar in class, so I saw his phone all last week. He and half the boys are in a fan war against the followers of another actor. At first it was only jokes and funny edits, and Tushar laughed so hard he wheezed.
Then the comments changed. He typed something nasty under a rival fan’s photo, and the group chat filled with cheering replies. Imran, sitting beside him, did not reply at all and just kept scrolling.
Tushar looked thrilled, as if he were on a team in a real match. Later the rival fan wrote, “Why are you all so mean?” Tushar went quiet. I can’t know what he felt, but he locked his phone.

qa.q: How did the fan war begin, according to Deepika?
qa.a: It began as jokes and funny edits, and Tushar laughed so hard he wheezed.

qa.q: What might Tushar have felt when the group chat cheered his nasty line?
qa.a: He may have felt thrilled and part of a team, since he looked as if he were in a real match. The cheering rewarded him for going further.

qa.q: What could Tushar try when the banter starts to hurt someone?
qa.a: He could stop typing and picture the rival fan reading the words. Then he could decide whether the line is still a joke or has turned into cruelty.

qa.q: How might Imran, who kept scrolling, have seen the fight?
qa.a: Imran may have felt uneasy about the cruelty but did not want to break the group's mood. The passage shows only that he did not reply, so his reason is a guess.

grounding: Shows a teenage fan joining a fan war that slides from joking into cruelty, seen through an observer's account.

passage:
Monday. Sahil’s group of school friends posted jokes about a rival star’s new film, and rival fans posted jokes back. Sahil laughed at every reply and felt part of a team.
Wednesday. The jokes got sharper. Sahil posted an edited photo mocking how a rival fan looked, and the chat filled with “savage” and “more!” Chetan did not reply.
Friday. The rival fan, a girl, wrote, “I thought this was about films.” Sahil’s stomach dropped. He typed a mean answer, then deleted it. Chetan sent him a private message: “Bro, that one went too far.”
Sahil looked at the message for a long time, then took the photo down.

qa.q: What did the rival fan write on Friday?
qa.a: The rival fan wrote, “I thought this was about films.”

qa.q: Why did Sahil delete the mean answer he had typed?
qa.a: Sahil's stomach dropped when he saw that the rival fan was hurt. The cheering had made him feel like part of a team, but her message made him see a real person.

qa.q: What made Chetan's private message a good move?
qa.a: Chetan did not shame Sahil in front of the group. A short private message made it easier for Sahil to step back.

qa.q: How might the rival fan have felt seeing the edited photo and the cheering replies?
qa.a: She was likely hurt and outnumbered. Her reply, that she thought it was about films, shows she expected fun and got mockery instead.

grounding: Shows a teenager enjoying a fan war with friends as banter turns into cruelty, and then noticing the harm.

passage:
Yamini, you asked about my favourite singer, so here goes. I’m Disha, and I was fifteen, and I’d played her album every night for two years. Last month a report said she had treated her staff badly for a long time and hidden it.
First I refused to read it. Then I read it and felt sick. I didn’t delete the songs, because a couple of them got me through exams. But I stopped posting her lyrics.
When my friends said, “People exaggerate,” I said, “The songs are still good, and what she did is still wrong.” Nobody answered. Holding both things feels strange, but pretending felt worse.

qa.q: How old was Disha when the album played every night?
qa.a: Disha was fifteen and had played the album every night for two years.

qa.q: What was Disha feeling after reading the report?
qa.a: Disha felt sick, which shows how much the singer had meant to Disha.

qa.q: What choice did Disha make about the songs, and why did it work?
qa.a: Disha kept the songs but stopped posting the lyrics. That kept what was good in the music without excusing what the singer did.

qa.q: What might Disha's friends who said people exaggerate have been feeling?
qa.a: They may have been trying to protect their own admiration, or avoiding the discomfort of the report. Their silence after Disha's answer suggests they had no ready reply.

grounding: Shows a teenager working through disappointment in an admired singer, keeping the music without excusing the wrongdoing.

passage:
Kishore had a poster of an actor above his desk. When news broke that the actor had shouted at junior crew members and then apologised in a half-hearted way, Kishore stared at the poster for a long time. I’m Karthik, his classmate, and I was next to him.
Manoj said, “So what? Everyone does that.” Kishore said, “Not everyone.” Ayesha stayed silent and looked at her notebook.
That evening Kishore said, “I still like the films. What he did to those people isn’t okay, and I’m not going to pretend it is.” He took the poster down and slid it inside his cupboard door. I couldn’t tell whether he felt sad or angry.

qa.q: What did the actor do that upset Kishore?
qa.a: The actor shouted at junior crew members and then apologised in a half-hearted way.

qa.q: What might Kishore have been feeling as he stared at the poster?
qa.a: Kishore was probably disappointed, since the actor had been someone he admired. Karthik could not tell if it was sadness or anger, so both are possible.

qa.q: Which choice of Kishore's showed he could keep the good and still be honest?
qa.a: He said he still liked the films but refused to pretend the behaviour was fine. He then took the poster down rather than arguing about it.

qa.q: How might Ayesha, who stayed silent, have seen the exchange between Manoj and Kishore?
qa.a: Ayesha may have agreed with Kishore but felt it was hard to speak against Manoj, or she may have been unsure. Looking at her notebook shows she stayed out of it.

grounding: Shows a teenager, seen by a classmate, working through disappointment in an admired actor without excusing the behaviour.

passage:
Monday, in the hostel canteen, Rafiq showed Vikas an article that criticised the star Vikas adored. “Fake,” Vikas said before he reached the second paragraph. Neha and Sam, at the same table, kept eating and said nothing.
Wednesday, late at night. Vikas replayed the star’s interview clips and felt as if the star were speaking straight to him. He typed a long reply to a stranger who had criticised the star.
Saturday. Rafiq asked lightly, “Would he even know your name?” Vikas snapped, “That’s not the point,” and walked out. In the corridor his chest felt tight, as if Rafiq had said something about him.

qa.q: What did Vikas say about the article on Monday?
qa.a: Vikas said, “Fake,” before reaching the second paragraph.

qa.q: Why did Vikas's chest feel tight after Rafiq's question?
qa.a: Criticising the star felt like criticising Vikas, and the question about being known touched something painful. His snapping reply and tight chest suggest hurt more than anger.

qa.q: What small step could help Vikas after that Saturday?
qa.a: Vikas could read the article slowly and separate what it says about the star's actions from how he feels about himself. He could then decide what he still admires.

qa.q: How might Rafiq have felt after Vikas walked out?
qa.a: Rafiq may have felt surprised and a bit guilty, since the question was asked lightly and a strong reaction was not expected. The passage does not say for sure.

grounding: Shows a young adult defending an admired star automatically because criticism feels personal, with a one-sided closeness.

passage:
Yash, come and sit. When I was twenty, I loved a film hero more than my own opinion. I’m Preeti, and I can say that now, but then I couldn’t. My college friend Anita once said his latest film was dull, and I didn’t speak to her for a week.
I wrote him a letter and never got a reply. I read every magazine and felt he knew me. Anita just waited. After a week she came with two tickets for his next film and said, “Let’s watch, then argue.”
In the dark I saw the same dull scene she meant. I said nothing, but my face was hot.

qa.q: How long did Preeti stay silent with Anita?
qa.a: Preeti did not speak to Anita for a week.

qa.q: Why did Preeti's face feel hot in the dark theatre?
qa.a: Preeti saw the same dull scene Anita had meant and felt uncomfortable because Anita had been right. Admitting it would mean the hero was not perfect.

qa.q: Which choice of Anita's helped Preeti most?
qa.a: Anita waited a week and then brought two tickets and proposed watching first and arguing later. She kept the friendship without forcing Preeti to admit anything.

qa.q: How might Anita have felt during that week of silence?
qa.a: Anita may have felt hurt and puzzled that a small opinion cost the friendship. Waiting and then bringing tickets suggests she still valued Preeti.

grounding: An elder recalls idealising a film hero so strongly that criticism felt personal, until a friend's patience opened a gap.

passage:
Dear Tenzin,
I’ve been meaning to write since Sunday’s listening party. When I moved into the hostel in a new city, I ate dinner alone for a month. Then I found our fan group online and you, Mira and Joel wrote to me.
Someone drew my favourite character. Someone else shared a playlist when I had a bad week. On Sundays we listen together and talk about anything. When a group from another band mocked us, you said, “Let them be. We’re here for the songs.”
It’s the first place here that felt like mine. Thank you for that. ❤️
Sabina

qa.q: How long did Sabina eat dinner alone after moving to the hostel?
qa.a: Sabina ate dinner alone for a month after moving into the hostel.

qa.q: What was Sabina feeling before finding the fan group?
qa.a: Sabina was lonely in a new city, which is why the group felt like the first place that was Sabina's own.

qa.q: What did Tenzin's reply to the mocking group show about how the fan group works?
qa.a: Tenzin answered the mockery calmly and said they were there for the songs. It shows connection here does not depend on hating anyone.

qa.q: What might Joel or Mira have felt on hearing Sabina's message?
qa.a: They may have felt glad and a little proud that the group made a lonely person feel welcome. The letter thanks Tenzin mainly, so their feelings are a guess.

grounding: Shows a young adult finding connection and comfort in a fan community during a lonely time, without hatred of others.

passage:
Salma, you asked how the forum started. I’m Binita, and it was my first year at a university abroad, and I didn’t know anyone. My roommate was away most weekends, and evenings felt very long.
I started reading a forum for a detective series I loved. Then I posted a short story about one of the characters, and three strangers replied within an hour. One of them, Ines, started editing my spelling with jokes. After that we wrote stories together.
Once somebody posted hateful things about another series’ viewers, and the moderators deleted it and wrote, “We don’t do that here.” I stayed. I’m still there, and I’m still writing.

qa.q: What did Binita post that got replies from strangers?
qa.a: Binita posted a short story about one of the characters in the detective series.

qa.q: What was Binita feeling in the first weeks abroad?
qa.a: Binita felt lonely, since nobody was familiar and the evenings felt very long.

qa.q: What did the moderators' response to the hateful post show that helped Binita stay?
qa.a: They deleted it and said such posts were not allowed. That made the forum feel safe and showed connection did not depend on hating others.

qa.q: How might Ines have felt when the story-writing with Binita began?
qa.a: Ines probably felt welcomed and playful, since Ines replied so quickly and joked while helping with spelling. It suggests Ines also enjoyed finding someone to write with.

grounding: Shows a young adult finding connection and creative outlets in a fan forum during lonely first-year months.

passage:
Tuesday. Kashish saw the review of a singer’s new album pop up in a group chat with Himani. Within an hour the fans had turned on the reviewer, calling her ugly and stupid. Himani, usually gentle, added a cruel joke.
Wednesday. Someone posted a link to the reviewer’s workplace and made remarks about her family. Kashish felt sick. Kashish muted the chat, reported the posts, and did not reply.
Friday. Kashish and Himani had lunch together. “I saw you leave that chat,” said Himani quietly. “It felt like a game until the family part. I’m not sure why I joined in.”

qa.q: What did someone post on Wednesday?
qa.a: Someone posted a link to the reviewer's workplace and made remarks about her family.

qa.q: What was Kashish feeling when the family remarks appeared?
qa.a: Kashish felt sick. Muting, reporting and staying silent show Kashish did not want any part of it.

qa.q: What safe steps did Kashish take instead of joining or arguing in the chat?
qa.a: Kashish muted the chat and reported the posts without replying. Kashish later listened to Himani calmly instead of scolding.

qa.q: How might Himani have felt about the whole thing by Friday?
qa.a: Himani seemed uneasy and a little ashamed, saying it felt like a game until the family part. Himani was asking why the group made it easy to join.

grounding: Shows an adult seeing fans turn abusive online, recognising how group identity allows cruelty, and choosing not to join.

passage:
Dolma, this happened when I was your age. I’m Lokesh, and I belonged to a fan club for a famous batsman. A magazine writer said our hero was past his best, and our club president got furious.
At the Sunday meeting he said we should all write to the writer, as rude as we could. Everyone laughed and agreed. I sat silent, though my ears burned.
Afterwards I told our teacher-patron what was planned. The teacher called the president in. The letters were never sent.
Some boys avoided me for weeks. The writer never knew. I still think about how easy it was for everyone else to say yes.

qa.q: What did the club president want the members to do?
qa.a: The president wanted everyone to write to the writer, as rude as they could.

qa.q: How might the club president have felt when the magazine writer criticised the hero?
qa.a: The president was probably furious and felt personally attacked, since the club was built around the hero. Group loyalty made anger feel like duty.

qa.q: Which choice of Lokesh's stopped the letters, and what did it cost?
qa.a: Lokesh told the teacher-patron about the plan. The letters were never sent, but some boys avoided Lokesh for weeks.

qa.q: What might the magazine writer have gone through if the letters had arrived?
qa.a: The writer would have received a pile of rude letters for one opinion and would probably have felt targeted and unsafe.

grounding: An elder recalls a fan club planning to abuse a critic and choosing not to join, and quietly raising it with a trusted adult.

passage:
The small kabaddi ground behind the market was full on Sunday. Reena, who ran the tea stall by the gate, had cheered for the town team for twenty years. When they lost the semi-final, her fellow fans blamed the referee.
“The referee was fine,” Reena said, wiping cups. “Our coach kept the tired raider in too long.” A few people frowned. Others nodded slowly.
Hafsa, a supporter from the next village, was standing by with a friend, looking gloomy. “Tea?” Reena said. “On the house, for the walk home.” Hafsa laughed. “Your coach is still wrong.” “I know,” said Reena. “Come again next season.”

qa.q: Where did Reena run her tea stall?
qa.a: Reena ran the tea stall by the gate of the kabaddi ground behind the market.

qa.q: What was Reena feeling after the semi-final loss?
qa.a: Reena was probably disappointed but clear-eyed, still loyal to the team while seeing that the coach kept the tired raider in too long.

qa.q: What did Reena's offer of tea to Hafsa show?
qa.a: It showed that rival fans could still be treated as people. A free cup of tea after a match took the sting out of the rivalry.

qa.q: How might Hafsa have felt when Reena offered tea?
qa.a: Hafsa was probably surprised and warmed by it, since Hafsa laughed and joked about the coach. The gloomy look softened.

grounding: Shows a mature fan loving the town team while admitting its faults and treating a rival fan kindly.

passage:
After the derby, Esther stood at the bus stop in her club scarf, holding a cold coffee. Her club had lost three-nil. Around her, a few fans grumbled about the referee.
“No,” Esther said. “The referee was fair. Our manager should have changed the tactics at half-time.” A man near her scowled.
Nour, wearing the rival club’s colours, walked past with two friends, smiling like someone who’d won a bet. Esther nodded. “Well played. You deserved it.”
Nour stopped, surprised. “I thought you’d be furious.” “I am,” said Esther. “About my manager. Want to share a warm drink?”

qa.q: What was the score in the derby?
qa.a: Esther's club lost three-nil.

qa.q: What did Esther blame for the loss, and why was that notable?
qa.a: She blamed her own manager for not changing tactics at half-time and said the referee was fair. It showed she could stay loyal without excusing faults.

qa.q: What made Nour stop and turn around?
qa.a: Esther congratulated Nour instead of jeering or sulking. Nour had expected fury and was surprised.

qa.q: How might the man who scowled have felt about Esther's words?
qa.a: He may have felt annoyed that she criticised the manager or the fans' anger. The passage shows only his scowl.

grounding: Shows a mature fan loving a club while admitting faults and treating a rival fan as a person.

passage:
Friday. Chandrika noticed the colony park was full of wrappers and old bottles. She told her friends on the swings. “Who will clean it?” asked Hrithik. “We will,” she said.
Saturday. Six children turned up with gloves and cloth bags. Two uncles brought sacks and showed them how to separate plastic. Hrithik carried the heaviest bag and puffed. A small boy named Anand held the bag open with both hands, silent and proud.
Sunday. The park looked different. A little girl swung on the swings and laughed. Chandrika stood at the gate and grinned. “We did that,” she said quietly.

qa.q: How many children came to clean the park on Saturday?
qa.a: Six children turned up with gloves and cloth bags.

qa.q: How did Chandrika feel on Sunday when she saw the clean park?
qa.a: Chandrika felt proud. Standing at the gate and grinning, she quietly said that they had done it.

qa.q: What small step turned Chandrika's noticing into action?
qa.a: When Hrithik asked who would clean it, she said “we will” and invited her friends. That made it a shared job, not a complaint.

qa.q: How might Anand, who held the bag open, have felt?
qa.a: Anand probably felt proud to have a real job in the clean-up, since he held the bag with both hands, silent and proud.

grounding: Shows a child joining a clean-up drive with friends and feeling proud that together they made a difference.

passage:
Jahnavi, you asked why I keep this old school badge. Let me tell you. When I was ten, my class decided to collect used books for a village school. I’m Neelam, and I had never organised anything.
We borrowed a handcart. Ravi, the strongest boy, pulled it. A quiet girl, Divya, kept the list and ticked every house. I only knocked on doors and felt my knees shake.
By evening we had three hundred books. Our teacher looked at the cart and said nothing for a while. Then she smiled. Divya put her pencil behind her ear and we all laughed.

qa.q: What did Neelam's class collect?
qa.a: Neelam's class collected used books for a village school.

qa.q: How might Neelam have felt knocking on doors?
qa.a: Neelam was nervous, since the knees shook. Neelam had never organised anything before but kept knocking on doors anyway.

qa.q: Which choice by the class made the collection succeed?
qa.a: They divided the jobs: Ravi pulled the cart, Divya kept the list and Neelam knocked on doors. Each child did the part that suited them.

qa.q: What might Divya have been feeling as she ticked every house on the list?
qa.a: Divya may have felt proud and focused, since her quiet job kept everyone's effort organised. Putting the pencil behind her ear at the end suggests a happy, satisfied mood.

grounding: An elder recalls a childhood book drive with a class, where each child's small part added up to something real.

subtype: First cause a teenager cares about [Actor]
passage:
Vijay had one night left. The principal’s meeting was at nine the next morning, and his petition to ban plastic bottles in the canteen needed forty more signatures. He and Ganga stood in the corridor with clipboards.
A classmate, Ruchi, said, “I’d sign, but the refill station has been broken for weeks. Where will we get water?”
“That’s an excuse,” said Vijay. “You’re part of the problem.”
Ruchi’s smile vanished. Ganga said softly, “She’s asking a real question.”
Vijay’s ears grew hot. He wanted to argue, but he took a breath and said, “Okay. Let’s add the station to the petition.”

qa.q: When was the principal's meeting?
qa.a: The principal's meeting was at nine the next morning.

qa.q: What was Vijay feeling when he called Ruchi part of the problem?
qa.a: He was passionate and certain, under time pressure. In his mind anyone who disagreed was blocking the cause.

qa.q: What turning point helped Vijay change course?
qa.a: Ganga pointed out that Ruchi was asking a real question. Vijay took a breath and added the broken refill station to the petition.

qa.q: How might Ruchi have felt when Vijay called her part of the problem?
qa.a: Ruchi probably felt stung and unfairly blamed, since her smile vanished. She had raised a practical concern, not refused to help.

grounding: Shows a teenager passionate about a first campaign and certain that anyone who disagrees is wrong, then pausing to listen.

subtype: First cause a teenager cares about [Actor]
passage:
The lane behind Afreen’s building had no streetlight, and she was tired of walking home in the dark. She and five friends went door to door with a petition. By Saturday they had twenty-six signatures, and Afreen felt part of something big.
Mr. Bhatt on the ground floor refused to sign. “The society funds are low,” he said.
“He just doesn’t care about safety,” Afreen muttered.
Saurabh, one of the group, said, “Maybe he’s worried about the cost. Maybe we should ask how much.”
Afreen frowned, then knocked on Mr. Bhatt’s door again. “Can we show you the price?” she asked.

qa.q: How many signatures did the group have by Saturday?
qa.a: They had twenty-six signatures by Saturday.

qa.q: What was Afreen feeling as she muttered about Mr. Bhatt?
qa.a: She was frustrated and sure that he was wrong, and she felt the cause was a matter of safety. Her belonging to the group made disagreement feel like carelessness.

qa.q: What changed when Afreen went back to Mr. Bhatt's door?
qa.a: She stopped assuming he did not care and offered to show him the price. That gave him a chance to say what worried him.

qa.q: How might Saurabh have seen Mr. Bhatt's refusal differently from Afreen?
qa.a: Saurabh saw a possible money worry rather than carelessness. Saurabh asked how much it would cost, which shows a search for the reason behind the refusal.

grounding: Shows a teenager passionate about a local campaign who first assumes those who disagree are wrong, then listens.

passage:
I’m Akash, Arnab’s roommate. On Thursday he packed a water bottle, his ID card and a phone charger before breakfast. The campus march about hostel fees had been approved by the college office, and volunteers had a plan.
Arnab was very quiet. He called home, said only that he had exams next week, and hung up. His hands trembled as he tied his shoes.
He came back at dusk with a sunburnt face and a paper badge. “Everyone stayed calm,” he said. “I was scared at the start. Then a stranger shared her water.” I don’t know what he felt, exactly, but he was smiling.

qa.q: What did Arnab pack before the march?
qa.a: Arnab packed a water bottle, his ID card and a phone charger.

qa.q: What might Arnab have been feeling as his hands trembled?
qa.a: He was probably afraid, and also determined to go. His quiet manner and shaking hands showed fear, but he went anyway.

qa.q: What choices in the passage kept the march safer?
qa.a: The march had been approved by the college office, volunteers had a plan, and Arnab carried water, ID and a charger. Everyone stayed calm.

qa.q: How might the stranger who shared water have felt?
qa.a: The stranger may have wanted to make a scared newcomer feel welcome. Sharing water was a small, warm sign of solidarity.

grounding: Shows a young adult joining a peaceful, approved march with fear, pride and solidarity together, seen by a roommate.

passage:
Monday. Madhuri sat with her notes for the term exam and a message from the lake-protection group. A permit had been granted for a peaceful walk on Friday. Her friend Sudha said, “I’m going. Come with me?” Madhuri’s stomach twisted.
Thursday. She told her parents about it. They worried aloud, and she promised to stay near the organisers and leave if things turned tense.
Friday. The crowd was bigger than she expected. Her heart pounded, but organisers with armbands walked along the line and reminded people to stay calm. A stranger smiled and passed her a water bottle.
Saturday, she was back at her desk, tired and glad.

qa.q: What kind of event was Madhuri considering on Friday?
qa.a: It was a peaceful walk for the lake-protection group, and a permit had been granted.

qa.q: What was Madhuri feeling at the start of the walk?
qa.a: Madhuri was scared, with her heart pounding, and also proud to be there. The organisers' reminders and the stranger's kindness helped steady her.

qa.q: What choices did Madhuri make to balance the cause against the risks?
qa.a: She told her parents, promised to stay near the organisers and to leave if it turned tense. She also went with a friend to a permitted event.

qa.q: How might Sudha have felt when Madhuri said yes?
qa.a: Sudha was probably glad and reassured to have company. Sudha had invited Madhuri directly, so it mattered to her.

grounding: Shows a young adult weighing risk against a cause and joining a peaceful protest with fear, pride and solidarity.

passage:
“A rally? With crowds?” said Jeevan, putting down his tea. “Seema, you know how these things can go.”
Seema’s mother pressed her lips together. “And the photos. Who knows who will see them?”
Seema’s first thought was to snap that she was twenty and it was her decision. Instead she looked at their faces and saw fear, not anger. “I know you’re worried,” she said. “I am too, a little.”
She showed them the organisers’ number. “I’ll share my location, text you every hour, and leave if it turns rowdy.”
Her father nodded slowly. “Then I’d like to speak to the organiser first.”

qa.q: What did Jeevan say when Seema mentioned the rally?
qa.a: Jeevan asked, “A rally? With crowds?” and reminded Seema how these things can go.

qa.q: What did Seema notice in the faces of Jeevan and her mother?
qa.a: Seema noticed fear rather than anger. She saw that their worry was about her safety.

qa.q: What made Seema's response work better than defiance?
qa.a: She admitted she was a little worried too and offered a plan: share her location, text every hour and leave if it turned rowdy. That answered the fear directly.

qa.q: How might Seema's mother have felt when she said photos could be seen?
qa.a: She was probably anxious about reputation and about Seema being noticed by strangers. Pressing her lips together shows she was holding worry back.

grounding: Shows a young adult finding her mother and father anxious about safety and reputation, and calm conversation about risk helping.

passage:
“Simran, sit. Just for a minute,” said Amma.
“Amma, I’m going. I told you.”
“I’m not saying don’t. I’m asking what happens if the crowd changes.”
Simran breathed out. “I’m scared too, honestly. That’s why I’m going with the group from college, and Ritu’s cousin is one of the volunteers.”
“And you’ll call me when you get there?”
“And when I leave.”
Tejas, her younger brother, looked up from his book. “Can I keep the map with the leaving points?”
Amma almost smiled. “Fine. But you pack the flask, Simran.”

qa.q: Who is Tejas in relation to Simran?
qa.a: Tejas is Simran's younger brother.

qa.q: What was Amma really worried about when she said she was not saying don't?
qa.a: Amma wanted to know what would happen if the crowd changed. She was anxious about safety, not trying to forbid Simran.

qa.q: What turning point made the conversation calmer?
qa.a: Simran admitted she was scared too and explained the safety plan: going with a group, a volunteer contact and calling at arrival and departure.

qa.q: How might Tejas have seen the argument between Amma and Simran?
qa.a: He may have felt worried and wanted to help, which is why he offered to keep the map. It shows he understood that both cared about Simran's safety.

grounding: Shows a young adult whose Amma is anxious about protest, and a calm family conversation about risk helping more than defiance.
